questions.stem: In 1206 Temujin was proclaimed ruler of the united Mongol tribes. What title did he take?
options: Shah of Persia
Son of Heaven
Genghis Khan
Kublai Khan
questions.explanation: At a great assembly (kurultai) in 1206, Temujin was proclaimed Genghis (Chinggis) Khan, 'universal ruler'. Kublai Khan was his grandson, who later ruled China.

questions.stem: What kind of home did most Mongol families live in on the steppe?
options: A wooden hut raised on stilts above the flooded river plains
A round felt tent called a ger that could be packed up and moved
A stone longhouse with a turf roof, built to last for generations
A mud-brick house inside the walls of a large farming town
questions.explanation: Mongols were nomadic herders who moved with their animals between seasonal pastures, so they lived in gers (also called yurts) — felt-covered frames that could be taken down and carried on carts or animals. Stone longhouses with turf roofs belong to places such as Viking Iceland.

questions.stem: Why was the horse so important to Mongol life?
options: Nomads relied on horses for travel, herding, milk and warfare
Horses were sacred and could never be ridden or used for food
Horses pulled the ploughs on the large wheat farms of the steppe
Horses were traded to China in exchange for all Mongol food
questions.explanation: Children learned to ride very young, horses carried herders and warriors across vast distances, and fermented mare's milk (airag) was a staple drink. The dry grassland steppe was used for grazing, not for large ploughed wheat farms.

questions.stem: According to The Secret History of the Mongols, why was Temujin's early life so hard?
options: He was sent away as a boy to be educated by Buddhist monks
His family were rich merchants who lost everything in a flood
His father was poisoned and his clan abandoned the family
He was raised as a prince in the palace of the Chinese emperor
questions.explanation: The Secret History, the main Mongol account of his life, says his father Yesügei was poisoned by Tatars and the clan then left Temujin's mother and her children to survive alone on the steppe. He grew up in poverty, not in a palace.

questions.stem: How did Genghis Khan organise his army?
options: In units of 12, 144 and 1728 soldiers
In legions of about 5000 foot soldiers each
In units of 10, 100, 1000 and 10 000 soldiers
In units drawn from each soldier's own clan and family
questions.explanation: The army used a decimal system — the arban (10), jaghun (100), mingghan (1000) and tumen (10 000) — and Genghis deliberately mixed men from different tribes so loyalty went to him rather than to old clans. Legions were the units of the ancient Roman army.

questions.stem: What was the 'feigned retreat' used by Mongol armies?
options: Retreating to the steppe each winter to rest the horses
Sending fake messengers to ask the enemy for peace
Leaving a city empty so that the enemy would starve in it
Pretending to flee to lure the enemy into a trap
questions.explanation: Mongol horsemen would pretend to break and run; when the enemy chased them and lost formation, hidden troops and the turning riders surrounded and attacked them. The tactic relied on the discipline and riding skill of the horse archers.

questions.stem: The Yassa was:
options: a round felt tent used by herding families
a cavalry unit of ten thousand soldiers
a code of laws associated with Genghis Khan
a relay system of riders carrying official messages
questions.explanation: The Yassa was the body of laws and decrees linked with Genghis Khan, covering matters such as military discipline and punishments. The relay system for messengers was a different institution, the yam.

questions.stem: What was the Mongol yam?
options: The law code that Genghis Khan gave to all of the Mongol people
A tax charged on every caravan using the Silk Roads
A great assembly that chose each new Great Khan
A network of relay stations with fresh horses for messengers
questions.explanation: The yam was a chain of stations a day's ride apart where official riders could change horses, rest and get supplies, so messages crossed the empire remarkably fast. The assembly that chose a new khan was the kurultai.

questions.stem: How did the Mongols generally treat the religions of the peoples they conquered?
options: They forced every conquered people to convert to Buddhism
They banned all religious worship across the lands they ruled
They made Christianity the only faith allowed in the empire
They tolerated many faiths and often freed clergy from taxes
questions.explanation: Mongol rulers generally allowed Buddhists, Muslims, Christians, Daoists and others to practise their faiths, and often exempted religious leaders from taxes in return for prayers for the khan. Some later khanates adopted Islam or Buddhism, but there was no empire-wide forced conversion.

questions.stem: What was the Pax Mongolica ('Mongol peace')?
options: A period when Mongol rule made trade along the Silk Roads safer
A treaty in which the Mongols promised never to attack Europe again
A wall the Mongols built to keep traders out of their lands
A time when the Mongols stopped all trade with China
questions.explanation: Once the conquests were complete, one power controlled much of the route from China to the Black Sea, protecting merchants and travellers, so goods, ideas and people moved more freely across Asia. The peace followed great violence — it described stability under Mongol rule, not a promise to Europe.

questions.stem: In 1258 Mongol forces led by Hulagu captured and sacked which city, ending the Abbasid Caliphate?
options: Rome
Baghdad
Constantinople
Jerusalem
questions.explanation: Hulagu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, took Baghdad in 1258 and killed the caliph; the city, a great centre of Islamic learning, was badly damaged. Constantinople fell much later, in 1453, to the Ottoman Turks.

questions.stem: Kublai Khan founded which Chinese dynasty?
options: The Han dynasty
The Qing dynasty
The Yuan dynasty
The Ming dynasty
questions.explanation: Kublai Khan declared the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and completed the conquest of southern China by 1279, ruling from Khanbaliq (modern Beijing). The Ming dynasty was the Chinese dynasty that later drove the Mongols out.

questions.stem: Which Venetian traveller wrote a famous account of Kublai Khan's court in China?
options: Vasco da Gama
Marco Polo
Christopher Columbus
Leif Erikson
questions.explanation: Marco Polo described his years in Kublai Khan's China in a book that amazed European readers and later inspired explorers. Columbus, born in Genoa, owned and annotated a copy of Polo's book, but he lived two centuries later.

questions.stem: Marco Polo was amazed that in Kublai Khan's China people paid for goods with:
options: glass beads made by Mongol craftsmen
paper money printed by the government
gold coins stamped with the khan's portrait
silver coins brought from Venice by traders
questions.explanation: The Yuan government issued paper money, building on earlier Chinese practice, and Polo described it with astonishment because Europe had no paper money at all. Venetian coins were not the currency of China, though Polo was a Venetian himself.

questions.stem: Why did the Mongol invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281 fail?
options: Storms wrecked the fleets, helped by strong Japanese defences
Japan paid the Mongols a huge tribute to make them turn their ships back
Kublai Khan called them off to send his army against Egypt
The Black Death broke out among the soldiers before landing
questions.explanation: Japanese warriors resisted the landings and built defensive walls, and typhoons destroyed much of the invasion fleet, especially in 1281; the Japanese called the storms kamikaze, 'divine wind'. The Black Death did not appear until the 1340s, decades after both invasions.

questions.stem: After the 1260s the Mongol Empire split into separate khanates. Which of these was one of them?
options: The Golden Horde
The Holy Roman Empire
The Abbasid Caliphate
The Byzantine Empire
questions.explanation: The empire divided into the Golden Horde (ruling over the Rus lands), the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia, the Ilkhanate in Persia and Kublai's Yuan dynasty in China. The Abbasid Caliphate was the Muslim state the Mongols destroyed in 1258.

questions.stem: In 1368 the Mongol Yuan dynasty was overthrown in China and replaced by:
options: the Ming dynasty
the Han dynasty
the Song dynasty
the Qing dynasty
questions.explanation: Rebellions, floods and famine weakened Yuan rule, and the rebel leader Zhu Yuanzhang drove the Mongols out and founded the Ming dynasty in 1368. The Song dynasty was the one Kublai Khan had conquered in the 1270s.

questions.stem: How did the Mongol Empire help the Black Death spread in the 1340s?
options: Busy trade and travel routes across its lands carried the disease west
Its armies brought the disease home from their invasions of Japan
It brought black rats into Europe for the very first time
It closed the Silk Roads, causing a famine that turned into plague
questions.explanation: The Mongols linked China, Central Asia and the Black Sea in one network of trade and travel, which also let plague-carrying fleas and rats move west with caravans and armies. Black rats had lived in Europe since Roman times, so the Mongols did not introduce them.

questions.stem: Why are historians cautious about the huge death tolls given for Mongol conquests of cities such as Nishapur?
options: Modern archaeology has shown that these cities were never attacked at all
The figures come from Mongol records written to hide their own crimes
Modern DNA tests have proved every chronicler's figures to be exact
Chroniclers may have exaggerated, and no reliable count of the dead was made
questions.explanation: Medieval chroniclers often gave enormous round numbers to show horror or the scale of a disaster, and no one counted the victims, so historians treat the figures as signs of great destruction rather than exact totals. The massacres themselves are not in doubt — what is debated is how many died.

questions.stem: Why could a relatively small Mongol population conquer such a vast empire?
options: Firearms and cannons that none of their enemies had ever seen before
Armies that outnumbered every enemy by about ten to one
Enemies who all surrendered without fighting a single battle
Fast, disciplined cavalry, plus captured engineers for sieges
questions.explanation: Mongol horse archers were highly mobile and disciplined, and the Mongols recruited captured Chinese and Persian engineers to build siege engines for attacking walled cities. They were often outnumbered, and gunpowder weapons were first developed by the Chinese, not the Mongols.
